takeaway: GogetaFS merges deduplication fingerprints into file-system block mappings, persisting both metadata roles once and eliminating their separate crash-ordering path.
background: A deduplicating file system fingerprints blocks and redirects duplicates to one physical copy. Fast persistent memory and non-cryptographic hashes reduce fingerprint computation, exposing the cost of maintaining a persistent fingerprint-to-physical index alongside the file system's own logical-to-physical index.
villain: Traditional designs write fingerprint metadata before file mappings so recovery can repair reference counts. The extra small writes and ordering points consume 18–38% of I/O-path time, while merely replacing cryptographic hashes leaves this duplicated metadata path intact.
approach: GogetaFS stores a logical–fingerprint–physical entry in the file system's durable mapping and reconstructs a fingerprint-keyed table in memory. An on-storage fingerprint table reconciles block-level deduplication with extent mappings, while lock-free and memory-regulated index variants adapt to available DRAM. Existing file-system persistence supplies crash consistency.
impact: Merged metadata makes transparent deduplication closer to an ordinary file-system feature on fast media, reducing I/O amplification and simplifying failure recovery. The principle generalizes: when two layers persist mappings with a shared field, combining their durable representation can remove cross-layer ordering.

evaluation.overview: Synthetic and trace workloads measure basic throughput, deduplication-metadata time, I/O amplification, memory-regulated variants, recovery, and portability from persistent memory to an emulated ultra-low-latency SSD.
evaluation.implemented: A NOVA-based persistent-memory GogetaFS plus an F2FS port for an emulated Z-SSD; the LFP-specific F2FS changes are reported as about 50 lines, with deduplication logic modularized.
evaluation.setting: A 16-core Xeon Gold 5218 server with 128 GB DRAM and 512 GB Intel Optane DCPMM, plus FEMU Z-SSD experiments; FIO, backup, mobile, and server traces run with up to eight threads.

results.text: Across persistent-memory workloads, GogetaFS is reported to improve throughput over Light-Dedup by 5.6–35.0%, with especially large gains for 2 MB writes and deletions.
GogetaFS reduces measured deduplication-metadata time by 75.4–92.8% versus Light-Dedup and nearly eliminates added read/write bytes for 4 KB deduplication.

Failure recovery is reported as 9.5–30.8% faster than Light-Dedup because GogetaFS rebuilds deduplication state from file-system mappings rather than separately checking a persistent fingerprint table.

limitations: GogetaFS requires intrusive file-system integration and storage-specific memory regulation. Its non-cryptographic fingerprints require content comparison and can miss later duplicates after a collision. The prototype does not implement background re-deduplication, PM-to-DRAM hot-entry swapping, or efficient mapping updates for block migration; SSD results use emulation, and GogetaFS reaches 79–99.6% of plain F2FS there.
phd_group_signal: The work isolates a newly dominant cost after hardware acceleration, redesigns the persistent data model rather than optimizing around it, and evaluates recovery, memory scarcity, aging, and a second media class. That is a strong example of systems bottleneck migration and cross-layer reasoning.

claims.text: An LFP entry combines a logical block number, fingerprint, and physical block number so the file-system mapping's existing I/O and recovery path also persists deduplication metadata.
With an eight-byte non-cryptographic fingerprint, the paper's model finds LFP metadata smaller than the separate-mapping design below an 80% duplication ratio.
